archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-led)
archetype.definition: A division leader whose record rests on a top-five passing offense and a run-stuffing, short-area defense rather than on turnover luck, though the defense still leaks big plays downfield.

report.headline: A real offense, a bend-don't-break defense, and a division nearly in hand.
report.take:
Last year's 13-4 Jaguars were the luckiest team in football: first in wins over expected (3.87) with an offense that ranked only 13th in EPA. This year's 5-2 team is built differently and on firmer ground. The offense now ranks fifth in EPA per play, Trevor Lawrence has started every game, and the passing game (0.223 EPA a dropback, fifth) is doing the heavy lifting. Wins over expected sits at a modest 0.44. The record roughly matches the play, and the play is good. The point differential implies 4.6 wins, so they are maybe half a game ahead of themselves, not two or three.

What drives it is a clean split between the two sides of the ball. On offense, Lawrence spreads the ball: Parker Washington is the lead target, with Brenton Strange and Jakobi Meyers behind him. The run game works despite the line rather than because of it. Backs average only 1.8 yards before contact (30th), yet run success ranks eighth and short-yardage conversion second, which points to Bhayshul Tuten and a well-schemed ground game producing on their own. On defense, offenses can't run (rush EPA allowed -0.199, second) and can't win underneath (short-pass EPA allowed first in the league). That is why opponents pass against them more than almost anyone in neutral situations.

The numbers hide the deep ball. The same defense that smothers short throws ranks 29th in deep-pass EPA allowed and 29th against opposing WR1s per target. Points allowed look elite, but yards allowed sit in the bottom half. The gap is closed by a 40% red-zone touchdown rate allowed (fourth), a third-down defense ranked eighth and a plus-7 turnover margin. Those are the parts most likely to regress. The schedule also flatters them: the blowouts came against Cleveland, New England and Indianapolis, and the Philadelphia win came against an offense and defense now ranked near the bottom. The two losses, to Denver and Houston, came in games where the defense gave up 288 and 312 passing yards.

The direction is still clearly up. Houston, Indianapolis and Tennessee have a combined handful of wins, and two Titans games plus Indianapolis remain. The real risk is attrition. DaVon Hamilton and Eric Murray are done for the year, Antonio Johnson is out, and both running backs carry injury tags. A thinner secondary on a defense already vulnerable deep is the one trend worth watching.

strengths.title: Lawrence-led passing game is top-five
strengths.body: The offense's efficiency comes through the air: 0.223 EPA per dropback ranks fifth, and overall offensive EPA ranks fifth. That is a jump from 13th a year ago. The production isn't tied to one receiver, with targets spread across Washington, Strange, Meyers and Brian Thomas Jr. A distributed offense with a healthy starter tends to hold up.

strengths.title: Nothing works short or on the ground
strengths.body: Opponents get almost nothing from runs (second in rush EPA allowed) or quick throws (first in short-pass EPA allowed). This is structural: the front and underneath coverage force offenses to throw, which is why opponents' pass rate over expected against them ranks second. It should last, though losing DaVon Hamilton up front tests the run defense.

strengths.title: Wins built on efficiency, not luck
strengths.body: Unlike 2025's league-high luck number, this year's wins over expected is a modest 0.44. The point differential alone supports nearly every win. The one-score record is a neutral 0.5, so there is no pile of coin-flip wins waiting to flip back.

concerns.title: Deep-ball leak behind a thinning secondary
concerns.body: The defense ranks 29th in deep-pass EPA allowed and 29th in EPA per target to opposing WR1s. This is the cost of a scheme that squeezes everything underneath. It becomes more dangerous now that safety Eric Murray is out for the season and Antonio Johnson is out this week. Good passing teams have already found it: Cincinnati threw for 428 yards in a game Jacksonville barely won.

concerns.title: Points allowed flattered by red zone
concerns.body: Points allowed ranks near the top while yards allowed sit in the bottom half. The difference is a 40% red-zone touchdown rate allowed and a plus-7 turnover margin. Both tend to drift toward average, so expect the scoring defense to look more like its yardage numbers over the second half.

concerns.title: Penalties and a line that leaks
concerns.body: The offense commits penalties at a bottom-third rate, and line penalties rank 25th. Two games ran past 100 penalty yards: Cincinnati (125) and Philadelphia (100), both one-score wins. Backs also get little room, averaging 1.8 yards before contact. This is a real flaw rather than a side effect of anything good, and it keeps inferior opponents in games.

trend.note: The quality has been consistent, but the margins have swung with the opponent. Blowouts came against weak offenses, while one-score games came against Cincinnati and Philadelphia and a shootout loss to Houston. The 42-7 win over Indianapolis out of the bye shows nothing has slipped.

nextGame.headline: Ravens likely down to their third QB on a Thursday short week
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville travels to Baltimore on four days' rest as an 8.5-point favorite, with a total of 42.5. The Ravens are 4-4 and closer to average than their name suggests: 18th in defensive EPA, 23rd against the run and 27th in deep-pass EPA allowed. Opposing WR1s have had more success per target against them than against any other defense. Baltimore's offense ranks eighth in EPA, but that was built largely with Lamar Jackson, and they were just beaten 36-10 by Buffalo.

Availability decides this one. Jackson is on IR after thumb surgery. Tyler Huntley (toe) "probably" won't play per Jesse Minter, which leaves Joe Fagnano, himself limited with an ankle. Guard Olaivavega Ioane and safety Jaylinn Hawkins are out. Tackle Roger Rosengarten, guard John Simpson, Roquan Smith, Trey Hendrickson and kicker Tyler Loop are all questionable. For Jacksonville, both backs (Tuten and Rodriguez), Meyers, guard Ezra Cleveland, Travon Walker and corner Jarrian Jones are questionable. Antonio Johnson is out, and Hamilton and Murray are lost for the year.

waysToWin.title: Make a third-string QB beat them
waysToWin.body: With Jackson out and Huntley likely sidelined, Baltimore's offense probably runs through Fagnano behind a line missing Ioane and possibly Rosengarten and Simpson. Jacksonville takes away the run and short throws better than nearly anyone. That forces a backup to win outside the pocket and downfield on a short week, behind a line already allowing a 24th-ranked sack rate.

waysToWin.title: Feed Washington against BAL's WR1 hole
waysToWin.body: Baltimore ranks last in EPA per target allowed to opposing WR1s and 27th in deep-pass EPA allowed. Parker Washington is Jacksonville's lead target, and the passing game ranks fifth in EPA. Hawkins is out at safety, so Lawrence should have shots available early to build a lead a backup QB can't chase.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yards
waysToWin.body: Jacksonville ranks ninth in special-teams EPA, while Baltimore ranks 23rd and may lose its kicker. On fourth-and-short the gap is wide: the Jaguars convert short yardage at the second-best rate, the Ravens at the 30th. In a low-total game, field position and drive-extending conversions add up.

waysToLose.title: Backfield injuries stall the offense
waysToLose.body: Tuten missed Monday's walkthrough and Rodriguez is limited, so the run game could be in third-string hands on a short week. Baltimore is weak against the run overall but allows few explosive runs (fourth) and hits quarterbacks at a sixth-ranked rate. A one-dimensional Lawrence behind a leaky, penalty-prone line is how a heavy favorite stalls.

waysToLose.title: A cheap deep shot vs thin safeties
waysToLose.body: The one thing even a backup can do against this defense is throw deep, where it ranks 29th in EPA allowed. With Murray done for the year and Johnson out, the Jaguars are shorthanded in exactly the spot they're weakest. One or two explosive completions could swing a game projected to be low-scoring.

waysToLose.title: Self-inflicted drives and short fields
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's penalties already turned the Cincinnati and Philadelphia games into one-score finishes. Flags plus a turnover giving Baltimore a short field is the most plausible route to an upset, because the Ravens' own offense may not sustain drives. The Ravens are just as sloppy (29th in penalties), so discipline is a real edge if the Jaguars keep it.

nextGame.watch: Who starts at quarterback for Baltimore, and whether Jacksonville's depleted safeties can keep a backup from hitting the deep ball that is this defense's one real hole.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense and the run-and-short-pass defense are sustainable. They come from scheme and a healthy starting quarterback, not from bounces. Expect the scoring defense to give back some ground as the red-zone stops and turnover margin drift toward average, and as the season-ending losses of Hamilton and Murray thin the front and the back end. The schedule is kind: two Tennessee games, Indianapolis and a Houston team that trails by three games. Only Chicago and Pittsburgh look like true tests, plus a Dallas offense ranked fourth that could exploit the deep-ball weakness.

This profiles as a double-digit-win division champion rather than a repeat of last year's luck-fueled 13 wins. The ceiling depends on whether the secondary holds up against good quarterbacks in December.
swingFactors: Safety depth after Murray's season-ending injury
Health of Tuten and the backfield

confidence.note: Seven games against a soft schedule; the efficiency is real, but injuries are piling up on defense.
